explanation: Fires on nouns naming a sports or recreation playing surface or venue: lawns, courts, golf course, pool, pitch, (home) ice, rinks, baseball field, track, runway. It is strongest when a sport or surface modifier comes right before ("tennis courts", "golf course", "swimming pool"), and moderate for stadiums, parks, playgrounds and roads. There are rare weak hits on code indentation.

Fires on the names of command-line programs, compilers and executables where a shell command is written out (./test.pl, g++, gcc, grails, java -, mysql -, su, aws, firefox -new-tab, hdparm), and on words describing such tools (compiler, command line tools, program). It is strongest at the start of the typed command in technical Q&A text.

Fires on subword tokens in the middle or at the start of words in Romance-language text (Portuguese, Spanish, French, Italian), e.g. 'j|oguei', 'Est|ou', 'consec|ut|iva', 'equiv|ocado'. It is strongest on word pieces that split a native word. Weak hits on English boilerplate and code punctuation are probably noise.

Fires diffusely on function words and connectives (commas, 'and', 'to', 'as') and on head nouns in descriptive or expository prose that lists attributes or benefits (product descriptions, medical introductions such as 'the most common cause', place descriptions). There is no sharp token identity. It responds to the middle of an elaborating clause.

Fires on tokens in the first few words of a document or section: the opening of an abstract, an introduction, or the sentence after a heading or title (e.g. 'of all', 'Noisy', 'Exposure', 'On 30 August 2010'). The position near the start of the text matters more than the token itself.

Fires on determiners and articles (la, o, da, esa, this, a) that begin a noun phrase after a verb or preposition. It is strongest in French, Spanish and Portuguese and in English 'such a', 'along with this', 'between a'. It is weak on the adjective or noun that follows.

Fires on the first subword token of a word split into pieces, usually a rare or technical word that starts with a common prefix-like fragment: 'unt'(old/imely), 'Dup'(lex), 'dub', 'det'(ente), 't'.co, 'Den'(ial). It is strongest on 'unt'/'Un' and on t/d-initial fragments.

Fires on function words inside evaluative or emphatic phrases where a degree or comparison is expected next: possessive 's ('New York's', 'aviation's finest'), 'what better', 'more likely', 'what does that even', 'actually means', 'one of the most', 'its share'. It is driven by an emphatic or comparative construction more than by one token.

Fires on the main verb (is, has, are, have, had, did) right after a sentence's subject noun phrase, especially when the subject is a named entity, brand or place at the start of a document or paragraph ('Kuala Lumpur has', 'Hackett is', 'The Straub family has'). It is weaker on mid-text subject-verb pairs and on the punctuation that closes an introductory phrase.

Fires on the word 'out', most strongly in 'out of' ('4.2 out of 5 stars', 'out of phase', 'hoisted out of the water', 'arising out of'), and more weakly on 'out' as a particle ('read out', 'passed out'). There are minor weak hits on other 'o'/'Aut' word starts.

Fires on prepositions and function words (in, on, that, to, as, into) in technical or software Q&A text, where they link to a location or context ('in http clause', 'sitting in the "Ended" state', 'a file in assets/', 'LICENSE file that'). There are also scattered hits on name and file-name fragments. Overall it is a diffuse mixture.

Fires on verbs, verb endings and function words in Spanish and Portuguese running text ('como', 'tiveram', 'será', 'es', 'foi', 'até', 'que', 'concluiu'). It is weaker on 'de/del' in Spanish names and does not fire on English text.

Fires on punctuation and syntax tokens inside source code, such as closing quotes, semicolons, '();', colons in object literals, template arguments and preprocessor identifiers ('__CC_ARM', '_MSC_VER'). It is strongest on structural tokens that close an argument or declaration in C/C++/C#/JS code.

A mixture: 'presidential' after Democratic/Republican, digits in years ('201|7'), 'or' in 'one or more'/'two or more', Japanese name fragments, and words like 'benefits'/'Security' in insurance contexts. There is no single shared trigger.

Fires on assorted tokens in first-person or conversational text ('I', 'am', 'to', 'out of bed') and on 'of' in court names ('Supreme Court of Wyoming'). It also hits header and include tokens in code. No coherent single feature is visible.

Fires on relative pronouns and clause connectors that start a subordinate or continuing clause after a noun or comma: 'which', 'who', 'where', 'so that', ', and', 'if'. It is strongest on 'which/who' right after a noun phrase describing an entity.

Fires on the second part of a compound modifier or descriptive spec phrase ('dual reel', 'cylindrical-bore', 'Oetiker-style', 'twin-site', 'high-performance', 'high affinity', '12,000 capacity', 'high quality'). It responds to the head of a technical or product attribute compound right after its modifier.

Fires on function words and tokens inside casual, colloquial or narrative storytelling (personal anecdotes, dialogue, profanity): 'thought for a second', 'piece of shit', 'first time in', 'put her hands on'. It is driven by an informal first-person or narrative register, not by a particular token.

Fires on the first subword of a split proper name or rare word, especially fragments starting with M/V/G ('Mal', 'Mar', 'Mall', 'Vo'(ivodeship), 'Mann', 'gl' in hemagglutinin, 'ag' in Astragali). It is strongest on name-internal pieces in foreign place and person names.

Fires on 'and' (and commas) that join the last item of a list of proper names, mainly judges in court-opinion headers ('Before X, Y and Z'), banks or company names, and on other tokens in legal-document header boilerplate (Asst., OPINION, THE UNITED STATES). It is weaker on generic coordination.

Fires on 'date(s)/dating' in the sense of historical origin ('dates back to', 'dates from', 'origins date back'), and moderately on other phrases about how far back something goes ('going back to', 'as far back as', 'since 1971', 'genesis').
